title: The countryside that shaped me – and why it matters to us all

content.content: This post has been written by one of the members of the Environment Blog team. We wish to share some of our own experiences with nature to encourage you to get outside and explore your local environment. Please feel free to share your stories of connecting with nature in the comments section.
I spent much of my childhood in a typical English village between York and Harrogate.
Beyond it stretched the Vale of York, flat as a pancake beneath an enormous sky and not far from Marston Moor, site of one of the defining battles of the English Civil War.

The Vale’s fertile soils support cereals and other crops, leading it to be described as Yorkshire’s breadbasket. It is a reminder that the countryside is not simply somewhere to admire or visit. It is a working landscape, supporting food production, businesses and livelihoods. Farmers and land managers are central both to our food security and to the stewardship of much of England’s natural environment.

The landscape around our village was not dramatic in the conventional sense. But long walks with our border collie, Sam, along lanes, footpaths and field edges instilled a great appreciation of the countryside and nature of this country that has never left me.

We followed the meandering River Nidd, and sometimes swam in it during the summer, as it made its way towards the Ouse at Nun Monkton, with its large village green, grazed by free roaming cattle, and duck pond. We spoke to anglers along the banks and asked what they had caught: roach, dace, chub, barbel and perch. There was even a local legend about a canoeist losing part of a finger to a particularly formidable pike.
We explored local woodlands and natural ponds, where we saw the various stages of a frog’s life, from tadpole to hopping out of the pond.

Walking, cycling, exploring and being outdoors gave me exercise, freedom, curiosity and a sense of perspective. Although I wasn't consciously aware of connecting with nature, looking back the physical and mental benefits were clear.
Living and working landscapes

We were lucky to be close to two of our amazing National Parks – the Yorkshire Dales and the North York Moors – as well as other designated Protected Landscapes, including Nidderdale National Landscape, which includes the incredible geological formations of Brimham Rock.
Together, National Parks and National Landscapes cover around a quarter of England. In North Yorkshire, Protected Landscapes cover more than 47% of the county.
My first overnight stay with a friend away from home was at Grinton Lodge Youth Hostel, near Reeth in Swaledale, for a weekend of mountain biking.
Although nature spotting wasn’t the primary purpose of the stay – I was focused on pedalling up hills in the rain – just being there strengthened an appreciation of nature and the habitats around us.

Swaledale takes its name from the River Swale, which supports brown trout and Atlantic salmon that migrate upstream to spawn in gravel-bedded tributaries. The Dale is also home to otters and birds including dippers, grey wagtails, kingfishers, curlews and lapwings, as well as species-rich wildflower meadows.

The bones of the Dales would have been recognisable a thousand years ago – the sweeping valleys, limestone scars and tumbling rivers – but their appearance would have been different. There would have been more woodland and fewer of the stone walls, barns and enclosed fields that now seem almost as ancient as the hills.
The Dales are not an untouched wilderness. Much of what we think of as their timeless character is the product of centuries of farming and land management.

Appropriate grazing can help maintain some open habitats; hay meadows support pollinators; healthy soils sustain food production; and peatlands store carbon, hold water and provide habitats for specialist plants and wildlife.

These landscapes are also economically important. Farms, shops, accommodation, hospitality and outdoor businesses all depend, directly or indirectly, on the character and health of the countryside. Protecting nature and supporting prosperous rural communities are not opposing ambitions: each depends on the other.
A treasure for everyone

The government’s 30by30 Delivery Plan sets out how farmers, land managers, businesses, communities and government can work together to effectively conserve and manage 30% of England’s land for nature by 2030.
Protected Landscapes will be central to that work, but designation alone is not enough. Habitats must be healthy, connected and resilient – and people must be able to experience and value them.

Our countryside is a national treasure. But it is also much more: a source of food and livelihoods, a home for wildlife, a store of carbon, a defence against floods and fires, and a place where people can breathe, move and find perspective.

I feel fortunate that these landscapes were part of my childhood. Those seemingly ordinary walks, bike rides and days beside the river helped shape who I am, and the connection they created has stayed with me throughout my life. Not everyone has the same opportunities to experience nature, which is why caring for the countryside must also mean helping more people feel that it belongs to them.

If we can do that, perhaps a child setting out today beside a river, across a field or through a local park will discover the same sense of freedom, wonder and belonging – and carry it with them for the rest of their life.

title: 'Slick and easy' cleaning services procurement with Get help buying for schools
authors: Nicola Wells, school business manager, Amery Hill Secondary School

content.content: Nicola Wells is the school business manager at Amery Hill Secondary School – a single academy trust in Hampshire with approximately 1,000 students. Here she shares her experience of using Get help buying for schools to procure cleaning services for the school.
We were looking to run a cleaning tender, as we were in the final year of our three-year contract with our current supplier.

I’d previously been involved in a school collaboration for a tender run through Get help buying for schools, which had gone really well – so it seemed like the perfect opportunity to use the service for our cleaning procurement.

We decided to use Get help buying for schools for several reasons. Cost was a huge factor – the fact it was free was amazing. It also ensured compliance and gave me peace of mind knowing that all the companies offering frameworks had been checked by the Department for Education and had agreed to certain service levels. It made the process easy for us as a school, and it was quick.
Brilliant support from start to finish
I was a bit concerned I’d left it too late, but we managed to make the schedule work for both us and the Get help buying for schools team – and the service was brilliant.

I’d done some research online and had a framework in mind. We went through the process to gain access to the frameworks, and everything went smoothly from there. It was very simple and straightforward.

The support was brilliant from start to finish. The response times were really quick, and the team were so helpful. I had a few questions once I took over the process myself, and they answered clearly. Everything from getting the specification ready, to going out to tender, to help with questions on the portal and scoring – it was all so slick and easy.
Fantastic free service

The outcome was great. We had weighted the tender 40% on cost and 60% on quality, so I knew we might pay a bit more, but quality was the biggest factor for us as we wanted to raise our cleaning standards in the school. The successful company started not too long ago and we’re really happy – on both sides.

Get help buying for schools saved me so much time as a school business manager. They support you through the whole process, and at no point did I feel like I was on my own. It hasn’t cost the school any money either. The fact that it’s a free service is fantastic.

I would definitely use the service again for other areas in our school. If you’re a school considering using Get help buying for schools, I’d highly recommend it. The process is fair, professional, and offers a huge amount of support. It’s definitely worth it from a cost-saving perspective too.

title: Dragons' Den IP Blog - Series 23 Episode 10

content.content: Picture this: the lift starts to rise. Your heart is racing, the nerves are kicking in, and there's no turning back. The doors open and five familiar faces are waiting.
It's time for BBC Dragons' Den. The Dragons are ready, and this week's entrepreneurs are about to make their pitch. The question is, will they leave with an investment or face a fiery rejection?

As always, we'll be taking a closer look at the intellectual property (IP) behind the pitches, exploring the designs, patents and trade marks that help protect the innovations of tonight's hopeful entrepreneurs.
Music to the Dragons' ears

One entrepreneur hoping to strike the right chord with the Dragons was Tolu Farinto, founder of Limitless Live, a company creating free live music experiences for young people through brand sponsorships.
He entered the Den seeking £50,000 in exchange for 10% of his business.
Tolu explained how Limitless Live works with major brands to fund live music events, helping young people access experiences they may otherwise be priced out of.
Centre stage trade marks

Alongside delivering live events, Limitless Live has also taken steps to protect its brand. A quick search of the UK trade mark register shows that the business has registered trade marks for both LIMITLESS FESTIVAL and Limitless Live.

A registered trade mark can help protect the identity of a business and distinguish its services from those of competitors. If you're building a brand of your own, it's worth considering whether trade mark protection could form part of your IP strategy. You can search the trade mark register yourself and explore our free trade mark guidance to learn more.
Unfortunately Tolu left the Den without investment; however, he didn’t leave empty handed. He left with some great advice from Dragon Steven Bartlett on how to grow his business.
The secret ingredient

Later in the episode, entrepreneur Abilasha Bhohi entered the Den seeking £75,000 in exchange for 15% of her all-natural ice cream business, Moonji. Inspired by her British Indian heritage and her mother's cooking, she explained that she is currently producing small batches herself but is ready to take the next step and move production into a factory environment.

Scaling up production is an exciting milestone for any growing business, but it can also raise important IP considerations. When a product's success relies on a unique recipe, formula or process, protecting that valuable know-how should form part of the growth plan.

Unlike trade marks, patents and designs, trade secrets are not registered. Instead, they can protect commercially valuable information that gives a business a competitive advantage, provided it is kept confidential. Recipes, ingredients, manufacturing methods and formulations can all fall into this category.

If Abilasha decides to work with manufacturers or external partners to produce her ice cream at scale, she may need to share information about how her products are made. Before doing so, businesses should consider what measures are needed to keep that information confidential. Non-disclosure agreements (NDAs), confidentiality clauses in contracts and limiting access to sensitive information to all except those who need to know, can all play an important role in helping to protect trade secrets.

Abilasha left the Den with investment from Peter Jones and Tinie Tempah, who offered the full £75,000 but for 15% each, taking a combined 30% stake in the business. Abilasha accepted the offer and secured the backing she was looking for to help take the business to the next stage.
Have you protected your innovation?
While the Dragons were deciding where to invest their money, I found myself asking a different question: how are these businesses protecting what makes them unique?

This week's episode offered a reminder that IP comes in many forms. From copyright protecting creative works, to trade marks safeguarding brands and trade secrets preserving valuable business know-how, IP can help businesses build value, attract investment and support long-term growth.
If you're building a business of your own, now is a good time to think about what IP you have and how it could be protected.
Our free step by step guidance can help you identify, protect and make the most of your intellectual property.

title: Updating the supplementary codes for right to work and right to rent to version 1.1
categories: UK digital verification services trust framework

content.content: We have published new, 1.1 versions of the supplementary codes for digital right to work and right to rent checks, to align the rules with the upcoming changes to the right to work and rent regulations.
These 1.1 supplementary codes immediately replace the 1.0 supplementary codes published on 9 June 2026, which had not yet come into effect.
1.1 supplementary codes are to be used with the 1.0 trust framework
The new, 1.1 supplementary codes came into force on 2 September 2026, upon the accreditation of a conformity assessment body (‘CAB’) to certify against them. Their coming into force coincides with:

The gamma (0.4) versions of the right to work and rent supplementary codes will remain valid for now and providers will uplift to the new supplementary codes following the same uplift approach as for the 1.0 trust framework.

This means DVS providers who uplift their trust framework certification from gamma to 1.0 can uplift their certification against the right to work and/or right to rent supplementary codes directly from gamma to 1.1.
Any DVS who are not currently certified against the right to work or rent supplementary codes must undergo certification against the 1.1 versions if they want to be certified.

The changes between the 1.0 and 1.1 are described below. They are designed to give DVS providers more options, not fewer, so those that those who were working towards the rules in the 1.0 versions will be able to meet the rules in the 1.1 versions.
1.1. supplementary codes support changes in right to work and rent regulations

Publishing the 1.1 supplementary codes ensures the new right to work and rent supplementary codes are in force in time for regulatory changes that will take effect on 1 October 2026 following a statutory instrument laid on 30 June 2026.

Those regulatory changes mean that, where employers and landlords use a digital verification service (DVS) to check right to work or right to rent, they must use a digital verification service that is certified and registered against the DVS trust framework and the relevant supplementary code in order to obtain a statutory excuse.
The amended regulations will also:
1.1 supplementary codes enable a wider range of identity-checking methods
The 1.1 supplementary codes enable DVS providers to start conducting checks using the expanded document sets and reverification routes as soon as the regulatory changes take effect.
They do this by making three changes.
Recently expired documents

The 1.1 codes permit the use of passports and passport cards that have expired within the previous six months for right to work checks, provided a chip read is used as part of the document validation. This enables a wider range of evidence to be used by DVS, whilst safeguarding against the risks of expired document acceptance.
Simplified data outputs

The new codes no longer require that the identity profile and authenticator quality be shared by the DVS to the employer or landlord. Instead, a confirmation of registration, alongside a confirmation that the supplementary code was followed during the check, will be shared.

This change is intended to simplify the DVS output. If a provider is certified against the supplementary code at the time they conduct a right to work or rent check, and registered as such, then the employer or landlord can be sure the right identity and authenticator rules have been met.
Expanded role for holder services

The new right to work supplementary code will allow holder service providers to conduct checks to confirm that an individual carrying out work or services has previously had a successful right to work check.

This will enable DVS to be used for continuous checks, for example under the new regulations regarding extended liability, where workers may need to demonstrate to someone other than the employer with whom they have the direct contractual relationship that they have already undergone a right to work check.
Your involvement continues to shape the supplementary codes
In advance of publishing the 1.1 supplementary codes, we welcomed feedback on the working drafts, which informed the final version we have published this week.
We now welcome any feedback on the 1.1 supplementary codes.
Where you would like clarification on what the new rules mean in practice, let us know, as we would like to explain the changes further in upcoming blog posts.

And, as with the trust framework and its supporting documents, we’d like to hear where you think we could improve the rules themselves to make improvements in the future versions of the supplementary codes. To do this, we will continue to gather feedback through open engagement.

title: Commencing transition from 0.4 to 1.0
categories: UK digital verification services trust framework

content.content: Commencement of the transition period between the 0.4 and 1.0 versions of the trust framework and supplementary codes starts today
One of the conformity assessment bodies that are approved to certify against the UK digital verification services trust framework and the supplementary codes is now accredited to certify against:
In June, we set transition timelines for certified services as well as those that wish to get certified in the near future. These transition timelines commenced on 2 September 2026.

We have separately posted about the publication of the 1.1 versions of the right to work and right to rent supplementary codes, which are to be used with the 1.0 trust framework, and services uplifting their right to work or rent supplementary code certification from the 0.4 version will uplift directly to the 1.1 version.
What does it mean for you?

The CAB’s accreditation to certify against the 1.0 publication of the trust framework, and the 1.0 and 1.1 publications of the relevant supplementary codes, means that the transition period has begun as specified in section 0 of each publication.
Each service already certified has a minimum of 15 months to transition.

If your service currently holds certification against the 0.4 version of the trust framework, and/or the 0.4 versions of any of the supplementary codes, you should start thinking about when you would like to uplift its certification to the 1.0 version (or 1.1 version, in the case of the relevant supplementary codes). The options you have are outlined below.
Certification against the 1.0 version of the trust framework will also entitle you to use the CertifID trust mark.

If you have a new service that has not yet been certified against the trust framework, or an existing service that no longer holds a valid certification, you will follow the standard certification route.
Uplifting an existing certified service to 1.0
An approved and accredited CAB can certify your service against the 1.0 trust framework, and the 1.0 and 1.1 publications of the relevant supplementary codes, from 2nd September 2026.
All existing services will have a bespoke timeline for transition, based on their existing certification cycle. Every service will have at least 15 months to uplift.
If your service is already certified when the 1.0 trust framework comes into force, then:
By an “evaluation activity”, we mean either a surveillance audit or a full audit for services currently certified against the trust framework.
The same applies if your service is certified against the 0.4 version of one of the supplementary codes when the 1.0 or 1.1 versions come into force.
If you are certified against the 0.4 version of the DBS supplementary code, you will transition to the 1.0 version in the same fashion as for transition between the 0.4 and 1.0 trust framework.

If you are certified against the 0.4 version of the right to work and/or right to rent supplementary code, you will transition to the 1.1 version in the same fashion as for transition between the 0.4 and 1.0 trust framework.
You can choose to uplift sooner via a delta assessment
If you wish to uplift your service to the 1.0 trust framework sooner than your next evaluation activity you may be able to do so via an out-of-cycle delta assessment.
A delta assessment will only evaluate the rules that have changed between 0.4 and 1.0; it is not a full, top-to-bottom audit of your service.
Delta assessments are only available if your service:
You won't be able to have a delta assessment if your service is on a two-year cycle.

This delta assessment does not replace your ordinary cycle of evaluation activities. It will focus solely on the new requirements of the 1.0 trust framework. It enables you to make a choice of uplifting sooner than the service’s existing certification cycle, if you wish to.
New services
As of 2 September 2026, the 1.0 versions of the trust framework and DBS supplementary code, and the 1.1 versions of the right to work and right to rent supplementary codes are in force.
If your service is not currently certified and you want it to be, you will be evaluated against the in-force versions.
Start preparing for uplift
If you are a service provider, it is your responsibility to plan for and manage your uplift.
You should start to implement the 1.0 trust framework in your service from today, so you are ready to uplift. You should do the same for the 1.0 and 1.1 supplementary codes, as applicable.
You should also speak with your CAB to agree a plan for evaluating your service(s).
We believe this transition process gives every service provider a flexible, responsive uplift process that can meet its needs. If you have any questions you can contact either OfDIA or your CAB.
Services certified against 1.0 get a trust mark

We are very excited for this new trust framework, not only because it reflects the input from the industry and other key stakeholders, but also because certification against the 1.0 trust framework means issuance of the trust mark to services certified and registered against this version.
This is an exciting step for the ecosystem as the trust mark is another way of increasing trust in services that meet the requirements set by OfDIA.

title: Tony and Marian make the case for nature to Parliament's Environmental Audit Committee

content.content: This blog is a summary of Marian Spain and Tony Juniper's appearance in front of the Environmental Audit Committee, and reflections on their time in office.

Natural England's Chair Tony Juniper and Chief Executive Marian Spain appeared before Parliament's Environmental  Audit Committee this week, reflecting on the organisation's achievements over recent years and making a strong case for why nature must remain at the heart of the country's future.

The special session in the Houses of Parliament gave Marian and Tony the opportunity to look back at their time leading Natural England, while answering questions from MPs on some of the biggest issues facing nature and the organisation today.

Over almost two hours, the discussion ranged widely: from the condition of protected sites and species recovery to planning reform, water quality, climate change, resourcing and the role a healthy natural environment plays in economic growth and national security.
One message ran consistently through the session: nature is not a barrier to the things the country needs to achieve. It is fundamental to achieving them.
Looking back at how far we've come
Tony opened the session by reflecting on the transformation Natural England has undergone since he and Marian began working together in 2019.
He highlighted the development of a much clearer strategic direction for the organisation, increased investment and a renewed confidence in Natural England and its role.

He also pointed to the breadth of work delivered over that period: supporting the development of Environmental Land Management and Landscape Recovery; finding new approaches to enable development while protecting nature; tackling nutrient pollution; expanding National Nature Reserves; recovering species including beavers and white-tailed eagles; connecting more people with nature; and delivering major national trails.

Marian reflected on how this work has culminated in Natural England's current strategy, Recovering Nature for Growth, Health and Security, and the shift it represents in how the organisation talks about its mission.

Nature, she told the Committee, should not be viewed simply as something that needs protecting. Healthy and resilient ecosystems provide essential services on which our economy, health and security depend.

Marian and Tony's message to those who will lead Natural England in the future was clear: keep pushing in that direction, and keep making the case for nature as essential national infrastructure, rather than a "nice to have."
Nature and growth: moving beyond the false choice
A significant part of the discussion focused on economic growth and the persistent suggestion that protecting nature can stand in its way.
Both Marian and Tony strongly challenged that premise.

Marian stressed that Natural England recognises the country needs new homes, clean energy and infrastructure. The organisation's role is not to prevent that development, but to help ensure it happens in the most nature-friendly way possible, protecting the natural systems that the economy itself ultimately depends upon.

Tony described the idea that the country must choose between economic development and nature as a "false choice," pointing to evidence that investment in nature can create economic value and make communities and infrastructure more resilient.
Wetlands, woodlands, healthy coastlines and other natural assets, he argued, need to be thought about in much the same way as other infrastructure: investments that deliver a return for society.
Preparing for a changing climate
Following one of the hottest summers on record, the Committee also explored the impact of climate change and how nature can help the country adapt.
The discussion highlighted the role of green spaces, trees, water and other nature-based solutions in cooling communities, managing flood risk and making places more resilient.
Marian also drew attention to the inequality in access to nature and green space, and how communities with the least access can often be among those most exposed to the impacts of extreme heat.
Programmes such as Nature Towns and Cities demonstrate how investment in greener places can simultaneously support climate resilience, people's wellbeing and local economic growth.
A reflection of the whole organisation

While this session focused on Marian and Tony's leadership, many of the achievements discussed are ultimately the result of the expertise, commitment and hard work of Natural England colleagues across the country.

From people working with farmers and land managers to those advising on planning and infrastructure; from scientists and specialists to colleagues working on species recovery, protected sites, access, green infrastructure and partnerships, the session provided a powerful reminder of the extraordinary breadth of what Natural England does.
Closing the hearing, Committee Chair Toby Perkins MP thanked Marian and Tony not only for their evidence, but for their contribution to Natural England over the past seven years.

As Marian prepares to leave Natural England at the end of September and Tony approaches the end of his term as Chair next year, this session provided an opportunity to reflect on what has been achieved, but also on the scale of the task still ahead.
The central message was perhaps the simplest one of all: recovering nature isn't separate from delivering the future the country needs.
It is one of the foundations on which that future depends.

title: Shaping the future under uncertainty: the challenge of transformation

content.content: Climate change, energy security, artificial intelligence, demographic change and public service reform are among the defining policy challenges of our time.Addressing them requires more than incremental improvements. It requires transformational change - action that reshapes the systems, behaviours and incentives that determine long-term outcomes.
Whether decarbonising the economy, adapting public services to demographic change or harnessing artificial intelligence, the effects of these interventions can unfold over decades.

Yet policymakers must make decisions today based on assumptions about how the future will develop. Doing so is particularly challenging for transformational projects, which, by definition, are designed to reshape the systems, behaviours and incentives that drive future outcomes. Because they seek to change the very conditions on which forecasts are based, their long-term impacts and value are inherently uncertain.
Responding to the challenge
Across government, there is growing recognition that appraisal and decision-making approaches must evolve to meet this challenge.
At the centre of this effort is HM Treasury's Green Book, which provides guidance on how departments assess the costs, benefits, risks and wider impacts of policies, programmes and projects.

Recent developments, including the 2025 Green Book Review, place greater emphasis on risk, non-monetisable impacts and strategic objectives. They recognise transformational decisions cannot always be captured through simple benefit-cost ratios alone, particuarly when outcomes are uncertain and unfold over long periods.

This reflects a broader shift in how policymakers think about decision-making under uncertainty. Transformational decisions are often characterised by deep uncertainty, where future conditions cannot be predicted with confidence. For issues such as climate change, artificial intelligence and demographic change, the challenge is not to forecast a single future, but to consider how different futures might emerge.

As a result, public sector appraisal is being asked to place greater emphasis on longer-term public value, resilience and adaptability alongside traditional measures of value for money, supporting decisions that remain robust as circumstances evolve.
Appraising transformational change

Additional challenges in appraising transformational policies arise from their potential to create system-wide impacts and wider societal effects. These effects may extend across interconnected sectors and stakeholders and can be difficult to identify, quantify and compare consistently within appraisal frameworks.

These implications may include benefits such as resilience, wellbeing, environmental improvements and long-term economic adaptability. Such benefits can be central to a policy's overall value but may be more difficult to assess consistently within conventional appraisal approaches.

Decarbonisation provides a useful illustration. Future benefits depend not only on future climate policy and technological progress, but also on how households, businesses and markets respond to policy interventions. As behaviour and incentives change, the assumptions underpinning initial forecasts may themselves evolve, creating a wider range of possible future outcomes.
These characteristics of transformational investments - involving system-wide impacts, long time horizons and deep uncertainty – therefore require a broader approach to appraisal.

Approaches such as scenario analysis, stress testing and adaptive planning can help decision-makers understand how policies may perform under different future conditions. Rather than seeking a single "best estimate" of the future, these methods help evaluate the robustness of decisions across a range of plausible outcomes.
The actuarial contribution
Many of these approaches draw on capabilities that are familiar to actuaries.

Actuaries routinely work with uncertainty, long time horizons and complex systems. Whether assessing pension liabilities, insurance risks, climate-related exposures or the implications of demographic change, actuarial work often involves evaluating how different future scenarios could affect outcomes. Actuaries are also practiced in effectively communicating how decisions impact across a range of possible futures.

Tools such as scenario analysis, stress testing and long-term modelling are already widely used within the profession. These techniques can provide valuable insights for policymakers seeking to understand the implications of uncertainty and the trade-offs associated with different strategic choices.As governments confront increasingly complex and long-term challenges, these skills become increasingly relevant. By bringing a structured approach to uncertainty, risk and resilience, actuarial thinking can help support more informed and adaptable decision-making.
Looking ahead

The Green Book Review marks a new approach to appraisal in the public sector. Public-sector appraisal must be able to capture transformational change, wider societal impacts and long-term value alongside traditional measures of value for money.

Important challenges remain, however. While there is growing recognition of the need to consider uncertainty, resilience and broader public value, incorporating these factors consistently into decision-making remains difficult. Further work will be needed to develop frameworks that are robust enough to reflect these considerations while remaining proportionate and practical for routine use across government.

The debate is no longer whether uncertainty matters, rather it is a question of how best to account for it. In this context, the government continues to develop its approach to transformational policymaking. Green Book reforms and emerging professional thinking provide a stronger foundation for making decisions with long-lasting consequences. Getting these decisions right matters because they will affect citizens, public services and the wider economy for generations.

Ultimately, the goal is not to predict the future perfectly, but to make decisions that remain credible, resilient and adaptable as circumstances evolve. By being robust across a range of possible futures, well-designed policies today can help shape a better future tomorrow.

title: Should I be concerned that an invasive mosquito species has been detected in East London?

content.content: The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has detected Aedes aegypti mosquitoes and larvae at residential properties in East London. It is the first time this species has been found breeding in the UK, and the fourth modern-day detection of Aedes aegypti in the country overall. The initial finding was reported through UKHSA's Mosquito Watch surveillance scheme. Control measures have already been implemented to destroy the larvae and reduce the risk of further breeding, and we continue to monitor the area closely.
What is Aedes aegypti?

Aedes aegypti, sometimes called the yellow fever mosquito, is found across tropical and subtropical regions of the world. It's capable of transmitting diseases including dengue, chikungunya, yellow fever and Zika virus in places where those infections are already circulating, and where the weather can support transmission. It does not carry malaria.

The species thrives in warm, tropical climates and has historically struggled to adapt to the UK's temperate weather, and to survive our winters. For this reason, it is not expected to become permanently established in England, and has not managed to survive the winter anywhere in northern Europe. However, mosquitoes can adapt quickly. Early detection and swift control measures remain essential.
How worried should I be?

The risk to the public from this finding is assessed as very low. There is no evidence that these mosquitoes have caused any human infections, and to date there's no evidence of the mosquitoes or larvae being found in nearby public areas.

Invasive mosquitoes typically arrive in the UK by hitchhiking in vehicles, baggage or imported plants. Despite the evidence of breeding in this local area, and recent heatwaves, Aedes aegypti is not established in the UK and cannot survive long-term in the UK's overall climate, which remains too cold. The only places these mosquitoes currently survive in Europe are in some localities in the Mediterranean. That said, UKHSA expects that as the climate warms, incursions of invasive mosquitoes including the tiger mosquito, Aedes albopictus, and reports of them surviving here for longer periods, will continue.
How does UKHSA monitor for invasive mosquitoes?

UKHSA's Medical Entomology and Zoonoses Ecology (MEZE) team coordinates invasive mosquito surveillance across England, working closely with local authorities and port health teams. Surveillance has been running since 2010 and focuses on high-risk sites likely to receive cross-Channel traffic, including airports, ports, service stations and distribution centres, as well as in urban areas with a suitable climate.

The main monitoring tool is the ovitrap: a water-filled trap designed to attract egg-laying female mosquitoes. These are checked biweekly between June and October, when mosquito activity is at its highest, and any samples collected are sent to UKHSA for analysis.

If invasive mosquito eggs are found, UKHSA entomologists and Environmental Health Officers follow the National Contingency Plan for Invasive Mosquitoes. This involves inspecting a 300-metre radius around the site for potential breeding grounds, such as puddles, buckets and tyres, and removing, draining or treating them. Adult mosquito traps are deployed to monitor the area, with targeted treatments used if larval mosquitoes are detected. Local teams also work with residents and businesses to raise awareness and reduce standing water, with monitoring continuing for several weeks to ensure the mosquitoes don't spread further.
A further surveillance method includes the Mosquito Watch programme – a citizen science scheme that receives images of nuisance biting mosquitoes.
What can I do to help?

As a precaution, people can reduce opportunities for all species of mosquitoes to breed by removing standing water from gardens and outdoor spaces. This includes removing water collecting in buckets, containers, paddling pools, plant pots, blocked drains, bins and other discarded items, as well as fitting proper lids to water butts; all of which can harbour mosquito breeding.

If you spot a mosquito, you can help UKHSA's surveillance efforts by reporting it through the Mosquito Watch scheme. Mosquito Watch helps UKHSA fill gaps in data on the distribution of British mosquitoes, understand nuisance biting incidents, and detect invasive species early.

You can report a sighting using the online form, and you can also post physical specimens. If sending mosquitoes by post, live specimens should first be placed in the freezer for 10 minutes to kill them, then packed into a crush-proof container and sent along with the reference number generated by the online form. Mosquitoes from different locations should be placed in separate, labelled containers.
Note that UKHSA does not routinely test submitted mosquitoes for pathogens and cannot provide advice on mosquito-borne illnesses through the scheme.

title: Connecting data to enable modern digital government
authors: Mark Durkee, Head of Data Architecture, GDS

content.content: Delivering better public services increasingly depends on organisations working together. Whether addressing challenges that span national government, local government or devolved authorities, organisations need to be able to share information, coordinate activity and act on a common understanding of people, organisations and places. Over the past year, a small discovery team in the Office of the Chief Data Officer has been exploring what this means in practice. We have been identifying the foundational data that is critical to creating public services that are simpler, more joined up and organised around the needs of people, organisations and places. This work forms part of the wider effort to build the longer term digital and data foundations that public service delivery depends on.  A real example: supporting children in their early years The value of this work becomes clear when looking at a real public service challenge. In June, the government launched the Early Years Kickstarter. The project is exploring how information held by different services could be connected more effectively. This could help ensure children receive the support they need to be ready for school. Information about children is often held in separate systems by different organisations and professions. This can make it harder to identify needs early and coordinate support effectively. Connecting relevant information, where appropriate, could help professionals build a more complete picture. This could enable earlier intervention and better outcomes for children and families. This reflects a wider challenge across government. In many cases, the foundational data needed to improve outcomes already exists. The difficulty is making that data easier to find, access and use consistently across organisational boundaries. The challenge and the opportunity The public sector holds vast amounts of information, but we still find it difficult to share and reuse that information effectively. Different services often maintain their own versions of the same data. This creates duplication, makes collaboration more difficult and can lead to frustrating experiences for citizens and businesses. Our discovery found that some data sets play a particularly important role because they are used repeatedly across many services and organisations. We call these foundational data. Foundational data can be thought of as a small set of core facts that many services rely on. These might include who someone is, which organisation they belong to or where a property is located. When those facts are accurate, trusted and reusable, organisations can spend less time recreating or validating information and more time delivering services. The public can also spend less time providing the same information repeatedly to different organisations. Other countries, including Denmark and Estonia, have demonstrated approaches to making trusted foundational data easier to discover and reuse while maintaining appropriate safeguards. Connecting information across government One of the clearest findings from the discovery is the importance of consistent ways to describe people, organisations and locations. These are among the most widely used forms of foundational data across the public sector. We identified a need for what we call reference spines. These are shared ways of confirming that the same person, organisation or place is being referred to across different systems. This could make it easier to connect relevant information when there is a lawful and legitimate reason to do so. For locations, much of the infrastructure already exists. The Unique Property Reference Number provides a common identifier for properties and locations across the public sector. However, its use is not yet consistent enough for organisations to realise its full value. For organisations, there is currently no widely adopted equivalent. Different parts of government identify organisations in different ways. This makes it harder to exchange information and provide effective services to businesses. Similar challenges apply to information about people. The aim is not to create new data sets or bring information together in one place. It is to make it easier for organisations to connect information where appropriate, reducing the need for citizens to provide the same details repeatedly to different services. This work must be underpinned by strong safeguards, transparency and clear accountability. Information should only be connected where there is a lawful basis, a clear public benefit and appropriate oversight. These principles are fundamental to maintaining public trust. A federated approach One of the strongest conclusions from the discovery is that improving how organisations use data does not require the creation of a single, centralised database. The value comes from consistency, connectivity, standards and common approaches, rather than storing everything in one place. Common standards, interoperable data and stronger digital foundations all have an important role to play in enabling more joined up services across national, local and devolved government. Data sets should continue to be managed by the organisations best placed to maintain them. The challenge is to ensure that foundational data can be discovered, understood and reused more easily across organisational boundaries. This is not a simple task. Organisations are understandably focused on delivering their own services and priorities. As a result, it can be difficult to invest in data assets and capabilities that create benefits across the wider public sector. We therefore need an ecosystem that supports common ways of finding, accessing and using trusted foundational data while respecting existing responsibilities, devolved arrangements and local ownership. What comes next? The discovery has provided a clearer picture of the foundational data, products and capabilities that could support the ambitions set out in the Blueprint for Modern Digital Government. This work will help inform the development of the forthcoming government Strategic Data Roadmap, led by the Chief Data Officer and due to be published in the autumn. Modern digital government depends on trusted foundational data that can be discovered, accessed and reused across organisational boundaries. When organisations can work from the same reliable information, support can reach the right people more quickly, duplication can be reduced and services can become easier to use. Ultimately, this is not about data for its own sake. It is about creating the conditions for better outcomes for citizens, communities, organisations and places. Help shape this work You can help shape this work by providing feedback on the alpha Person Data Standard by emailing data-standards-authority@dsit.gov.uk.  You can send your feedback to the Data Standards Authority, via data-standards-authority@dsit.gov.ukIf you are a public sector data professional, you can also register for DataConnect26, taking place on 6 and 7 October. The event will bring together data leaders and professionals to discuss how better data can support growth, improve public services and deliver better outcomes for people and places.

title: From cadet to captain: a Merchant Navy story

content.content: To mark Merchant Navy Day on Thursday 3 September, we're shining a light on the seafarers who keep the UK supplied with the goods we rely on every day, and hearing from someone who spent nearly two decades living that life.

One of those seafarers is Shajan Lukose, Head of Nautical Examiners at the Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA). He spent 18 years at sea, rising to captain his own ship in 2000. He started his career in 1989 when voyages were longer and shore leave, unusual by today's standards, could stretch to three or four days. Shajan said:
"Today, because of containerisation, shore leave can be a luxury. It’s still a way to see the world and for most sailing the high seas is thrilling in itself "
For much of his career, Shajan was able to have his wife accompany him on voyages.

"It is possible for certain members of crew to have family stay on board with them and I was fortunate enough for this to be the case for me. Allocations are based on rank and are dependent on the numbers on the lifeboats for safety reasons."
Life on board in the 1990s meant no internet, no streaming content, and letters that sometimes waited at port for weeks. While times could be challenging, Shajan recalls the camaraderie this created:
Command brought real responsibility. In the early 2000s, Shajan captained a large crude oil carrier, taking oil from the Persian Gulf to Japan and the United States. He said:

"A single hull tanker, fully loaded, is like a seven-storey building below the water. Navigating the shallow waters of the Malacca Strait left no room for error, any slight touch on a rock and it would rip open."

While being the captain of a large vessel naturally comes with huge pressure, Shajan explained that all seafarers realise the responsibility they carry to look after their cargo, themselves and their crew.
Today around 90% of the UK’s traded goods are transported by sea. Shajan said:

"It's all made somewhere else, containerised and brought here safely, then unpacked straight onto the shelf. Cargo ships move fast too; the journey from Shanghai to Felixstowe takes around 20 to 25 days which just shows how quickly things reach the market."
Shajan explained that the discipline he learned at sea has never really left him. It's a mindset he still brings to his work at the MCA where he trains and examines the next generation of seafarers.
Merchant Navy Day 2026
This Merchant Navy Day, we recognise seafarers like Shajan, whose work, often unseen, plays a crucial role in keeping the UK supplied with goods.
Seafarers and organisations across the UK are encouraged to mark Merchant Navy Day 2026 by flying the Red Ensign and recognising the vital contribution of merchant seafarers.

title: Copilot and me: making the pace of work more manageable

content.content: I’m Leigh‑Ann Jones, a flood and coastal risk management (FCRM) advisor in the Environment Agency, working across digital, data and systems that support the FCRM capital programme.

Since 2023, Defra has been running targeted trials and rollouts of Microsoft Copilot – a personal AI assistant integrated into Microsoft apps. These pilots highlighted the meaningful ways it can benefit colleagues who are neurodivergent or have a disability or other access need. As such, Defra made full licences available as a reasonable adjustment earlier this year.

My role is pretty fast-paced and complex – there’s always a lot of detailed information and data to work through, alongside working with different stakeholders, providing technical support to colleagues and staff, among changing priorities.

I’m also neurodivergent (ADHD) and naturally think quickly and make connections easily. But turning that into clear, structured outputs can take more time and energy than you might expect. Sometimes I don’t have the knowledge needed to create the output I want to produce.
Help with overwhelm and task paralysis
My work is varied. I move between support, analysis and delivery, often all within the same day.

I might be supporting IT users through the service desk, working through emails and actions, joining meetings, looking at data, or getting into complex problem-solving and planning. I’m also involved in project delivery, including the replacement of AIMS:PD Project Online, our asset and project management system.

Because of that variety, I’m constantly juggling priorities and deadlines while trying to manage my own wellbeing. I’m taking in new information all the time, working out what matters most, and turning that into clear actions for myself and others.

On busier days, that can build up quite quickly. It can feel like my thinking slows down a bit, I start to feel behind, and that sense of overwhelm can creep in. Task paralysis can happen, and is difficult to deal with, but is often due to mental overwhelm, lack of information or coherent structure to get started from.

Copilot is there to help, and the full licence the Environment Agency has offered me provides AI support that understands my work context. I can tell it what is happening, share emails, documents, my action list – even talk to it. It helps me step back at that point, giving me a way to quickly make sense of everything, refocus, and bring some structure back before it starts to snowball and helps steer me away from rabbit holes. It can give me a way out of the woods, as it were, although I do love a good woodland walk.
Prioritising what matters

I mainly use Copilot in Teams, Outlook and Word to help me stay on top of all that information and decision-making. I use it to help with data insights in Excel and as a learning sidekick for Power Automate flow building.

It helps me quickly make sense of what’s coming in, whether that’s long email threads, meeting discussions or rough notes. From there, I use it to pull out key points and actions, turn notes into something clearer, and sense-check what I actually need to focus on.
A simple example is taking a long email thread or meeting notes and turning them into a clear summary with actions and owners. This now takes minutes instead of much longer.

More recently, I’ve started using Copilot notebooks, where I feed in relevant documents and context. That’s made a big difference. It means Copilot already understands the background, so the outputs feel much more useful and relevant. It’s not just helping me summarise things, it’s helping me think through what matters.

As the Inclusion and Accessibility Lead in our team, I have recently created an Accessibility Check Notebook, adding government guidance as sources of reference so that I can ask Copilot to check any SharePoint, Word, Email or Presentation content that I produce and suggest improvements, cutting out time consuming guidance checks back and forth.
Clarity, confidence and focus
Copilot doesn’t change how busy or complex my job is, but it really helps me stay ahead of what is important and what needs actioning or planning.
Instead of getting pulled into all the detail, I can get to what matters much more quickly and keep things moving.
Realistically, it’s saving me at least an hour a day just in working through emails.

It’s also been a game changer for meetings. Being able to use transcripts that show key moments – who said what and what actions came out of it – saves me several hours a week and means I’m much less likely to miss something important during the meeting because I can be present instead of writing down notes and trying to keep up with what is being said.
More than the time, it’s helped with:
Overall, it just reduces the friction in my day and makes things feel more manageable.
A ‘thinking partner’
What surprised me most is Copilot isn’t just a writing tool: it’s a thinking partner.
You don’t need to get it perfect to start with. Just begin with something rough and build from there.
Copilot is really helping to make the pace and complexity of my work more manageable. It helps me stay focused, up to date with what’s changing, and doing my best work more consistently.

title: Removing barriers to restoration: how your feedback is helping improve marine licensing
authors: Adam Tillotson, Regulatory Reform Unit Manager

content.content: Marine habitat restoration is essential if we are to reverse biodiversity loss and build resilience to climate change.

Across England, important habitats such as seagrass meadows, saltmarsh and native oyster reefs have declined significantly. Restoring them is vital for improving the health of our seas and coastal environment.

The Marine Management Organisation (MMO) has an important role in supporting restoration projects, while continuing to protect the marine environment. We know that regulation can sometimes feel complex, and we are working with Defra, Natural England and the Environment Agency to identify where improvements can be made.
Listening to restoration practitioners
In 2025, we asked restoration practitioners for feedback through a questionnaire promoted at the ReMeMaRe conference.

The responses provided valuable insight into the challenges applicants face when navigating the marine licensing process. They also highlighted practical improvements that could make it easier to deliver restoration projects.
This feedback builds on responses received through Defra’s consultation on marine licensing reform.
Improving guidance and support
One of the clearest messages from practitioners is that the marine licencing process can be difficult to navigate.
Applicants told us that they can find it challenging to:
Through the Marine Planning and Licensing Programme (MPLP), we are improving our guidance and digital service to help applicants find the information they need more easily.
‘Get permission for marine work’ can help you navigate through the process of applying for a marine licence.
Where applicants are unsure about project requirements, we encourage early engagement through our paid Pre-Application Advice Service.
The value of early engagement
Restoration practitioners also highlighted concerns about the time and cost involved in applying for marine licences.
In many cases, delays occur because important information is missing from an application or because issues arise during consultation that require further work.
Engaging early with the MMO can help applicants:
Although the Pre-Application Advice Service is chargeable, early discussions can help reduce uncertainty and avoid delays later in the process.
Tips for restoration projects
There are several ways applicants can improve the efficiency of the licensing process.
Engage early with advisers

Speak to key organisations, such as Natural England, the Environment Agency and Historic England, during the pre-application stage. Their advice can help shape project design and reduce the likelihood of issues being raised later.
Consider future project development
When planning restoration projects, consider whether activities may expand in future.
Applying for the full anticipated scope of a project, where appropriate, can reduce the need for licence variations later.
Take a strategic approach

If your organisation is planning multiple restoration activities within the same area over several years, it may be worth considering a single application that covers the wider programme of work. Although this can increase application complexity, it may reduce overall licensing costs and administrative effort.
What happens next?
This work is only the beginning.
We are continuing to work with Defra to review feedback from restoration practitioners and identify opportunities to improve the licensing experience wherever practical.

Missed us at ReMeMaRe 2026? Here's your chance to shape what comes next. We've launched a new questionnaire to find out how we can improve. Your input will directly inform our next steps, so please take a few minutes to share your views before the survey closes at the end of September 2026.

By listening to feedback and acting where we can, we aim to create a more transparent, consistent and effective marine licensing system that supports habitat restoration and helps nature recover in our seas and coastal environments.

title: Creating the best working environments for Civil Service in Greater Manchester

content.content: Greater Manchester and the Places for Growth programme

Greater Manchester is rapidly becoming a centre for digital and technology talent across government. It is a key location for the Civil Service’s Places for Growth programme which relocates thousands of roles outside of London.

With strong university links, a growing digital and technology workforce, and major government investment, including a new digital campus, Greater Manchester is a key location for creating opportunities for people to build careers in public service.

I'm a Data Analyst in Digital, Data and Technology based in our Greater Manchester offices, predominantly Trinity Bridge House. I also work as part of a committee to build a strong professional community, and most importantly offer our staff a sense of belonging.

If you’re looking to build a digital career in government outside London, our hub provides plenty of opportunities to grow and connect. Through a range of initiatives, we have made our community’s time in the office valuable and purpose-driven.
Trinity Bridge House

Trinity Bridge House is BIST’s main hub in Greater Manchester. It’s located right next to Salford Central train station, with our other sites positioned close to Manchester Piccadilly. All are within easy walking distance of the city centre. This gives colleagues quick access to Manchester’s shops, cafés and cultural scene, as well as excellent public transport links across the region.

Inside, the office is designed to support flexible, hybrid working. There are a variety of spaces to support both collaborative and focused individual work. Meeting rooms are equipped with high-quality technology for hybrid collaboration.

The building is shared with colleagues from HMRC and DESNZ, alongside dedicated areas for BIST teams. Our Manchester colleagues work across a wide range of roles; from technology and research to policy and logistics, collaborating closely with partners across the UK and internationally, including sector specialists and security experts.
Building a collaborative hub
Our committee built on the department’s commitment to making all offices collaborative and supportive places to work using:
Our approach combined lived experience, experimentation and input from across the community. We tested different ways of building connection, including:
This mix brought together multiple perspectives to better understand what people value in a workplace.
How we create meaningful connections for our Manchester staff
Several clear insights emerged. Some of our findings are supported by research around hybrid working and employee expectations, while others reflect emerging insight from local experience.
Physical presence alone does not create connection
With hybrid and distributed teams, offices need to actively facilitate interaction and design opportunities for connection beyond physical proximity.
Inclusivity is critical to participation
Traditional formats, such as evening socials, unintentionally exclude some colleagues. Offering a wider range of formats significantly increases engagement.
Professional and social value are closely linked
Activities that combine skill development with networking, such as coding sessions or profession-specific meet-ups, are especially effective.
Place matters
Being part of a wider Manchester-based Civil Service community, rather than a single office, helps create a stronger sense of identity and shared purpose.
What this means for our Manchester staff

The Places for Growth initiative has created opportunities for digital professionals across the UK, with many Civil Service roles being available outside of London and reducing the need for people to relocate.
Using our insights we have focused on creating opportunities to build local networks outside of DBT and enable skill and experience sharing in our hubs.
Thanks to our efforts, staff based in our Manchester hub get more than office space and role opportunities. They get:
Wider impact

Making roles available in more places widens the pool of applicants, helping the Civil Service attract and recruit stronger talent. The insights we’ve gained have broader implications for how the Civil Service approaches regional working. They suggest that investment in intentional cultural and community -building leads to greater collaboration and more attractive workplaces, especially outside of London.
This affects how we:

More widely, it reinforces the idea that both hybrid working and regional distribution are cultural changes, not just logistical changes. Organisations that succeed are those that design environments people actively choose to engage with.
What comes next?
In Greater Manchester, the direction is towards a more connected and consolidated hub model, bringing teams closer together while maintaining flexibility.
There is also continued focus on:
This is an ongoing process, with further growth and investment already planned.
Join a community in Manchester

With the rise of hybrid and distributed teams, the role of the office has changed permanently. In Greater Manchester we have shown that by providing more than a desk, we can transform the office from a workplace to a community.
By providing inclusive opportunities to connect, collaborate and learn, we can create places where people do their best work and feel part of something meaningful.
If you’re interested in being part of this journey, consider applying for roles in the Civil Service in Manchester.

How can you make your own team or workplace more intentional, inclusive and connected?
We’d welcome reflections, ideas and challenges.

title: Protecting UK democracy from hostile actors and foreign interference 🗳️🔒

content.content: The Government is taking further action to stop foreign money and hostile actors from interfering in UK elections and politics.

💪 Free and fair elections are the foundation of our democracy. Everyone should be able to trust that political decisions are made in the interests of UK voters, not people trying to buy influence from overseas.
What changes are we making this week? 📰

✅ We’re asking the Electoral Commission - the independent body which oversees elections - to look again at the limits on how much can be spent during election campaigns. We’ve also asked it to widen its review so it covers spending limits for individual candidates - not just parties and campaign groups.

✅ We’re planning a new test to stop wealthy people living overseas giving huge donations to political parties despite not living in the country. This will make sure donors have a genuine connection to the UK, rather than simply appearing to live here.
✅ A new team will be set up to look at other risks to UK democracy, such third-party campaigning, how transparent political funding is, and other emerging threats.
These plans build on action the Government is already taking through the Representation of the People Bill, which is returning to Parliament today with tougher rules on political donations.
Measures coming at Report Stage of the Representation of the People Bill 📜
Stopping overseas donors from giving unlimited amounts 🌍
✅ Voters who live abroad and want to donate to UK political parties will only be able to give up to £100,000 a year in total.

✅ If someone who lives abroad moves back to the UK, they'll still be limited to the £100,000 cap until they've been living here for a full calendar year. This stops people getting round the rules by moving home for a short time just to make a large donation.
✅ The same rule will apply to anyone moving to the UK for the first time, so people can't dodge the new rules by moving over before they come into force.
Banning donations made in cryptocurrency 💷
✅ Political parties will no longer be able to accept donations made in cryptocurrency. This applies to all cryptocurrency donations made from 25 March 2026 onwards, of any amount.
✅ Anyone who's already accepted a cryptocurrency donation will have 30 days to give the money back once the new rules come into force.
Making sure companies have a genuine UK link 🏢

✅ Companies wanting to donate to political parties will need to show they have a real and meaningful connection to the UK or Ireland. This stops shell companies being set up simply to funnel money from abroad into UK politics.

✅ Companies will only be allowed to donate up to the value of their post-tax profits each year, rather than being able to donate based on their total income. This closes a loophole that could let companies donate more than they can genuinely afford.
Beyond political finance: wider changes in the Representation of the People Bill 📜

The Representation of the People Bill doesn't just tackle foreign financial interference and political donations – it also includes several wider measures to modernise and protect UK democracy more broadly. Here's what else is included:
🗳️ Votes at 16: extending the right to vote to 16 and 17-year-olds.
📝 Improved voter registration: modernising registration systems, including making better use of data moving toward more automated processes.

🛡️ Harassment and intimidation: stronger protections and tougher sanctions to tackle harassment and intimidation of candidates and electoral staff, with wider work taking place through the Defending Democracy Taskforce, across government, police and the Electoral Commission.

title: GOV.UK Pay at 10: how it started and how it's going
authors: Alan Maddrell - Senior Content Designer for GOV.UK Pay, Government Digital Service

content.content: 10 years ago, GDS launched GOV.UK Pay, one of its flagship platforms used by public sector service teams. For the first time, public sector organisations could take payments without having to set up individual and costly transaction services themselves. Millions of people across the UK are now using GOV.UK Pay to quickly and easily pay for everything from a new passport to garden waste bin collections. By happy coincidence we have handled (nearly!) £10 billion in transactions, across almost 1,800 individual services in total. To mark this milestone, we look back at an incredible first decade and some exciting developments in store as we begin the next decade.
How it started
It's easy to forget what life was like before GOV.UK Pay:
In 10 years, we have solved these problems for more than 600 organisations across central and local government, the NHS, police, some educational institutions and the armed forces.
At first, we offered only API integration, so a technical team was needed to incorporate GOV.UK Pay into a service.
The first service to use GOV.UK Pay was "Send money to someone in prison", made by the Ministry of Justice. The transformation for them has been significant:
How it's going
This graph shows transaction volume over time from the start to the present day. It took GOV.UK Pay 4 years to collect its first £1 billion, it now processes this in around 5 months.
GOV.UK Pay's growth has been extraordinary, particularly since 2020.
This graph shows the top 10 organisations using GOV.UK Pay with their annual transaction volumes. The biggest user by some margin is HM Passport Office who joined in 2020.

HM Passport Office remains GOV.UK Pay’s largest service, with annual volumes of approximately 6.5 to 7.0 million since 2022, with a record of 1.11million monthly transactions in January 2023. Demand is highest in January and March (around 2.46 million transactions) before declining steadily towards the end of each year, reflecting passport renewal and travel-planning cycles. Volumes in January to July 2026 are 3.9% above 2025 (4.8 million), with HMPO’s overall platform share declining, which suggests growth across our other services.

That's only part of the picture, though, with hundreds of smaller organisations, including local authorities, now taking payments online. GOV.UK Pay is used by 41% (157) of local authorities across the UK, with 3.5m transactions processed in the 2025-26 financial year.
This graph shows the number of services created on GOV.UK Pay over time from 2016 to the present day.

When we introduced payment links in 2018, it became possible for a lot more teams to use GOV.UK Pay as illustrated by this graph. Payment links are quick and easy to set up and mean you don't need technical teams to develop and maintain a full online service.

We also survey our users regularly and the satisfaction rates show a net promoter score of +40. In the 2025 survey, 90% of respondents said they were very satisfied/satisfied with Pay, up from 83% in 2024. This shows that our public sector service teams appreciate GOV.UK Pay’s ease of use and not having to procure their own provider.
The future
There are some exciting times ahead. We are currently migrating to a new card provider, Adyen, for local authorities, armed forces and police.

We have ambitious plans to transform how services can take payments and save the taxpayer even more money in the process. This includes pay by bank, which we are making preparations for with ongoing migration to our new payment service provider Adyen. Keep an eye on our roadmap for further exciting updates.

As we close off the first 10 years, we want to say thank you to everyone who has worked on, used and supported GOV.UK Pay, past and present. It’s been an incredible journey so far and we’re as ambitious today as we were on day 1. Here’s to the next 10 years!

title: New duty takes effect to support children in temporary accommodation🏠

content.content: There are around 177,530 children living in temporary accommodation, the highest on record.

From today (1st September), a new duty takes effect, designed to enable these children to get the support they need as early as possible, and to stop vulnerable families from falling through the cracks.
WHAT'S THE PROBLEM? 📚
More families are living in temporary accommodation than ever before.
When a household is forced to move into temporary accommodation, it can be disruptive for children – affecting school attendance, healthcare appointments and access to support services.
Without the right join up between key services, support can come too late and children risk falling through the cracks.
The government wants to ensure that children experiencing homelessness receive the same opportunities and support as their peers, regardless of where they are living.
WHAT'S CHANGING? 🚀
From today, local authorities will be required to notify schools, GP practices and health visiting services when a child is placed in temporary accommodation.
To help councils implement the new duty quickly and effectively:
This means children staying engaged in education and ongoing connection to important health services – helping support wrap around families at the earliest stage.
HOW DOES THIS FIT INTO THE GOVERNMENT'S WIDER PLANS? 🏘️
The new duty is one part of the government's wider work to tackle homelessness and improve outcomes for vulnerable families.
It forms a key part of the National Plan to End Homelessness and sits alongside wider action to improve the experience of families living in temporary accommodation.
This includes £30 million of funding to reduce the use of B&Bs and improve the quality, suitability and long-term supply of temporary accommodation.

It also comes as the Prime Minister has launched a national drive to offer everyone sleeping rough a route off the streets this winter, backed by over £442 million to deliver more housing and specialist support.
It takes total investment in homelessness and rough sleeping services over the next three years to over £4 billion.
Reflecting on the news....
Homelessness Minister, Florence Eshalomi said:

“I know first-hand the uncertainty and upheaval that comes with not having a place to truly call home. For the thousands of children living in temporary accommodation, I know how much it can impact their school life, their ability to form lasting relationships and their sense of belonging.

“We’ve made clear that councils have a responsibility to place families in suitable, quality housing and from today, this will be matched with a new duty to inform education and health services when a child is homeless.

“This is a major milestone. Crucially, it means schools, GPs and councils all talking to each other about the vulnerable children in their community – ensuring vital support services are wrapped around them at the earliest opportunity and reducing the number of children falling through the cracks.”
Dr Laura Neilson, CEO of Shared Health Foundation said:

“I am delighted to see this notification be implemented. Education and health services want to support families living in temporary accommodation but have not known who the children are. That changes now.“I am grateful for colleagues in government and the civil service for their hard work and for the Minister championing this legislation. This is a key intervention to reduce the impact of homelessness on children, shine a light on them, and I believe it will save lives.”
Children’s Commissioner, Dame Rachel de Souza said:

“Every child deserves a safe, stable home and the opportunity to thrive, wherever they live. Children often fall through the gaps between services when they move between homes or move into temporary accommodation and face disruption to their education, healthcare and wider wellbeing.

“This new duty on local authorities is an important step towards making sure schools and health services know when a child moves into temporary accommodation, so they can put the right support in place. It is vital this duty is backed by a unique ID for every child, to help services join up information and ensure children do not lose access to the support they need whenever their circumstances change.”

title: Farmer Collaboration Fund: delivery partners can apply now

content.content: Delivery partners can now apply for the first round of the Farmer Collaboration Fund (FCF).
The £30 million fund will help farmers and land managers work together on local projects that improve productivity, sustainability and resilience.

Delivery partners are organisations with experience of supporting farmer collaboration. Funding will support them to establish new collaboration groups where there are gaps, support existing groups, appoint facilitators, share learning across the sector, and ensure funding is used effectively and transparently.
A summary of the fund
The FCF has been shaped through engagement with farmers, land managers and organisations across the sector.
At workshops held earlier this year, we heard that successful collaboration takes time and that groups need support to build relationships, develop shared priorities and turn ideas into action.

That's why successful delivery partners can receive funding for up to 3 years. This long-term approach reflects what we heard from farmers and gives groups the time and flexibility to develop projects that respond to local needs and opportunities.

For that reason, facilitators will provide direct support to farmer groups. They will co-ordinate meetings, arrange speakers and specialist advice, and help farmers agree shared actions. They may also support individual farmers where this contributes to the objectives of the wider group.

By working together, farmers can improve their businesses and deliver environmental benefits that would be difficult to achieve alone. This could include sharing machinery to reduce costs, adopting more efficient farming practices, and accessing funding opportunities such as Landscape Recovery.
Collaboration groups can also connect farmers with expert advice on issues including succession planning and business diversification.
To support collaboration and the sharing of ideas and experience, the FCF will fund activities including:
